justification_text:
The point estimates at each time horizon—1 day, 1 week, and 1 month—are all set to be the same value, 298.54. This reflects an assumption of stability in the underlying system or process being forecasted. Typically, such an approach may arise when there are no specific trends or strong directional factors driving changes in the variable being predicted, or when the most recent value (or average of prior observations) is assumed to represent the best central estimate for short- to medium-term horizons. It could also suggest that there's no immediate reason to believe the value will deviate significantly from the current state, at least under normal circumstances.

The confidence interval widths expand as the forecast horizon increases, which makes sense because uncertainty grows the further out you look into the future. Over one day, there is less time for unexpected shocks or random variations to influence outcomes, so the range from 293.57 to 303.51 is relatively narrow. Over a week, there is more time for cumulative uncertainty to play out, leading to the wider interval of 288.59 to 308.49. Over a full month, uncertainty compounds even further, reflected in the especially wide range of 278.54 to 318.54. Some of the sources driving this uncertainty could include variability in economic or market conditions, unexpected events, random fluctuations, or incomplete knowledge about underlying patterns and drivers.

Certain risks or events could push outcomes outside even the stated 90% confidence intervals. For example, major unpredictable shocks—such as geopolitical crises, severe natural disasters, sudden swings in policy, or unanticipated market volatility—could create feedback effects that aren't baked into the forecast. Similarly, if there are hidden structural shifts or rare but high-impact events not captured in historical data or the model assumptions, those could vastly skew results. Essentially, while confidence intervals give a likely range of outcomes, extreme tail events (sometimes called "black swan" events) are always a possibility. Over longer time horizons, such risks grow in magnitude, highlighting the inherent limitations of probabilistic forecasting.
